findings.finding: Two-minute quartet at quarter=55; first cello carries the highest line, with long exposed crescendos and no fast passagework.

grade.basis: Cached complete two-page score: slow whole-note chords and brief quarter-note motion; first cello reaches E4 above bass staff. Intermediate shifting and sustained tone, roughly RCM6/ABRSM5; ordinary chord tuning does not merit another level.

findings.finding: Four speaking violists; sampled pages rotate the melodic/textual role among players, with substantial contrapuntal and theatrical coordination.

grade.basis: Representative manuscript score pages 3,5,10: changing metres, syncopated independent lines, double stops, register and clef changes, tremolo and spoken Shakespeare integrated with playing. Instrumental demands around advanced level5; one ensemble level for coordinated speech, bow/pizz changes and displaced entries. Distributed featured lines make balanced more honest than a fixed first-viola lead.

findings.finding: Finale Allegro vivace supplies the main agility requirement across the three parts, led in range and sustained upper-line work by violin1.

grade.basis: Four-movement suite; sampled full finale spread (PDF5, printed8-9) shows rapid scale-like semiquavers, upper-register first violin, chromatic inflections, trills and articulated imitations. Around ABRSM7/RCM8 for the first player; conventional imitation and cadential coordination are included without uplift.

findings.finding: Three-movement ten-minute suite combines lyrical sustained upper voices with active lower figuration; all four violinists need articulate passagework.

grade.basis: Cached score PDF7 and10: first violin upper-register melody and repeated semiquaver figures; lower voices also have sustained semiquaver runs, second violin double-stop figuration. Early-advanced ABRSM7/RCM8 is proportionate to conventional tonal writing and shifting; no extra ensemble level for mostly clear shared pulse.

findings.finding: First violin rises to long high ledger-line notes in the central texture, while lower parts sustain rhythmic and tremolo motion; modern effects do not alone imply diploma difficulty.

grade.basis: Cached score PDF3 and6 with text-derived opening quarter=170: repeated eighth-note motor patterns and changing bow articulation, very high sustained first-violin line, tremolo, sul ponticello and dynamic extremes. Advanced ABRSM8/RCM9, led by first violin range; repeated patterns and common pulse keep ensemble demands inside this level.

findings.finding: The high first-cello line repeatedly crosses several ledger lines above bass clef at fast tempo; second cello closely follows and third provides an independent lower foundation.

grade.basis: Cached score PDF4 and first-cello part PDF6: Furioso quarter=144, changing7/8,6/8,4/4 and tempo returns; repeated high-register chromatic eighth notes, leaps and accented bowing reaching well into thumb-position territory. Pre-diploma cello level6 for sustained upper-register fluency; rhythmic coordination is significant but not enough for a further full level.

findings.finding: IRCAM and the composer association establish twelve cellos and eight minutes; technical evidence supports rapid spatial handoffs and sustained pitch-contour coordination rather than twelve conventionally doubling parts.
Cached Solomos monograph: printed p44 specifies circular onstage cellists; p63 identifies opening rotating heterophony built around three notes.

Solomos work-specific research analysis describes the central bars66–117 circulating one then two continuous glissando structures around the ring. This supports an explicit ensemble uplift; exact ranges and unseen score details are not claimed.
Institutional catalogue confirms1976, eight minutes,12 cellos, Salabert and Berlin Philharmonic members as premiere players.

grade.basis: Informed whole-work estimate, not full-score audit. Solomos research monograph (cached evidence, printed pp44 and63) identifies circular deployment and twelve-cellist rotating heterophony around three notes. His work-specific spatial analysis describes bars66–117 as interlocking continuous glissando rotations. The decisive challenge is precise distributed attack and glissando handoff across12 independent players: diploma-level specialist control plus one ensemble level yields professional8. No basis for extreme10 or assigning a uniquely hardest numbered cello without the score.
